questions.misconception_target: Treating Δh as either object's absolute depth instead of the vertical separation of the two pressure levels.
hints: Recall the previous lesson's relationship linking fluid density, gravitational field strength and a vertical separation.
The symbol after g describes the difference between two depth coordinates, not either coordinate alone.
walkthrough: The required hydrostatic relationship is Δp = ρgΔh.
Here Δp is the pressure difference and ρ is the uniform fluid density.
The separation term Δh is the vertical depth difference between the two levels.

ai_rubric.observable: States Δp = ρgΔh
Identifies Δh as the vertical depth difference between the two levels

questions.misconception_target: Assuming every fluid force on a submerged object points upward because the resultant is called upthrust.
hints: A pressure force is perpendicular to the surface it acts on.
For the top patch, decide which perpendicular direction points from the water into the object.
walkthrough: The patch is horizontal, so its normal direction is vertical.
The water lies above the top patch and pushes into the object.
The local force is therefore vertically downward, so option A is correct.

ai_rubric.observable: Selects A: the force is vertically downward and normal to the top patch

questions.misconception_target: Thinking horizontal pressure forces disappear because an upward force cancels them, rather than because opposite side forces cancel pairwise.
hints: Pair a small patch on one vertical face with an equal patch directly opposite it.
Compare their depths, pressures, areas and force directions.
walkthrough: Opposite matching patches are at the same depth, so the static-fluid pressure on them is equal.
Their areas match, so F = pA gives equal force magnitudes.
The normals point in opposite horizontal directions, so the forces cancel. Option C states this complete reason.

ai_rubric.observable: Selects C: matching areas at matching depths experience equal forces in opposite directions

questions.misconception_target: Assuming equal top and bottom areas guarantee equal pressure forces even though the faces are at different depths.
hints: Equal areas remove area as the cause of any force difference.
Use the remaining difference between the faces: their depths.
walkthrough: Hydrostatic pressure increases with depth, so the bottom pressure exceeds the top pressure.
Both faces have the same area, so F = pA makes the bottom force larger.
The bottom force is upward and the top force is downward, leaving an upward resultant. Option B is correct.

ai_rubric.observable: Selects B: the deeper bottom face has the larger pressure force, so the vertical resultant is upward

questions.misconception_target: Describing upthrust as one isolated force from below without accounting for the downward top force and cancelling side forces.

parts.misconception_target: Reversing the local force directions on the top and bottom faces.
hints: Draw each force perpendicular to its horizontal face and directed from water into the case.
Treat the top and bottom separately before thinking about the resultant.
walkthrough: The water above the top face pushes normally into the case, so that force is downward.
The water below the bottom face pushes normally into the case, so that force is upward.
These are the two required local directions.

ai_rubric.observable: States that the water force on the horizontal top face is vertically downward
States that the water force on the horizontal bottom face is vertically upward

parts.misconception_target: Claiming the side forces are absent instead of showing why present side forces cancel.
hints: Match a small area on the left face with the equal area directly opposite on the right face.
Use same depth to compare pressure, then use the face normals to compare directions.
walkthrough: Matching side patches are at the same depth, so each has the same water pressure.
The patches have equal area, so F = pA gives equal horizontal force magnitudes.
One force acts right and the other left, so their horizontal resultant is zero.

ai_rubric.observable: Explains that matching equal side areas at the same depth experience equal pressure and equal force
States that the two horizontal side forces act in opposite directions and therefore cancel

parts.misconception_target: Naming upthrust without stating that the pressure-force resultant is upward.
hints: Compare the downward top force with the upward bottom force after the side forces cancel.
walkthrough: The bottom face is deeper, so its upward force exceeds the downward force on the top face.
After the horizontal cancellation, the fluid-force resultant is upward.
This upward resultant is called upthrust.

ai_rubric.observable: Identifies the resultant as an upward upthrust

questions.misconception_target: Using pressure difference as if it were a force, or multiplying by the wrong geometric quantity.

parts.misconception_target: Substituting the 0.024 m² face area into the hydrostatic pressure-difference formula.
hints: The pressure stage needs density, g and the vertical separation only.
Keep the area for the next part.
walkthrough: List the pressure-stage data: ρ = 850 kg m^-3, g = 9.81 N kg^-1 and Δh = 0.18 m.
The unrounded result is 1500.93 Pa, which is 1.50 × 10^3 Pa to three significant figures.

ai_rubric.observable: Uses Δp = ρgΔh with 850 kg m^-3, 9.81 N kg^-1 and 0.18 m
Obtains a pressure difference of 1.50 × 10^3 Pa with a suitable unit

parts.misconception_target: Reporting 1500.93 as newtons without converting the pressure difference through the common face area.
hints: For equal top and bottom areas, subtracting pA on the two faces can be written as Δp multiplied by the common area.
Use the 0.024 m² value now and check that Pa m² becomes N.
walkthrough: Carry the unrounded pressure difference from (a): Δp = 1500.93 Pa.
ΔF = 36.02232 N, so the pressure-force difference is 36.0 N to three significant figures.
The unit check is Pa m² = N.

ai_rubric.observable: Uses the force difference ΔF = ΔpA with the common face area 0.024 m²
Obtains a pressure-force difference of 36.0 N with a suitable unit

parts.misconception_target: Giving an upward direction only because upthrust is expected, without linking direction to the deeper lower face.
hints: Identify which face is deeper and the direction of the force on that face.
walkthrough: The bottom face is deeper, so the liquid pressure there is greater.
Because both faces have the same area, the upward force on the bottom is larger than the downward force on the top.
Their force difference therefore acts upward.

ai_rubric.observable: Explains that the deeper bottom face has the larger pressure force, so the force difference acts upward

questions.misconception_target: Extending the equal-area shortcut ΔF = ΔpA to an unequal-area tapered object and ignoring vertical force components on sloping walls.

parts.misconception_target: Adding the two absolute depths instead of subtracting them to obtain the vertical separation.
hints: First find the separation between 0.65 m and 0.40 m.
Atmospheric pressure is common to both levels, so it does not enter their difference.
walkthrough: The vertical separation is Δh = 0.65 - 0.40 = 0.25 m.
Δp = 2452.5 Pa, which is 2.45 × 10^3 Pa to three significant figures.

ai_rubric.observable: Finds the vertical depth difference as 0.25 m and uses Δp = ρgΔh
Obtains a pressure difference of 2.45 × 10^3 Pa with a suitable unit

parts.misconception_target: Using ΔpA when there is no common A and treating the sloping walls as irrelevant because they are not horizontal.
hints: Write the two plate forces symbolically as p_top A_top and p_bottom A_bottom.
Ask whether a force normal to a sloping wall can have a vertical component.
walkthrough: For equal areas, p_bottom A - p_top A can be factored to ΔpA.
Here A_top and A_bottom differ, so that common-area factorisation is invalid.
In addition, every sloping wall experiences a normal pressure force with a vertical component.
The complete upthrust must therefore combine the plate forces and the side-wall vertical components.

ai_rubric.observable: Explains that unequal top and bottom areas prevent the two plate forces being written as one common area times Δp
Recognises that vertical components of pressure force on the sloping side walls also contribute to the complete upthrust

parts.misconception_target: Cancelling the entire two side-wall forces instead of cancelling only their equal opposite horizontal components.
hints: Resolve the force on each sloping wall into horizontal and vertical components.
Use symmetry to compare left and right components, then inspect their directions separately.
walkthrough: At matching depths, symmetric wall patches experience equal pressure-force magnitudes.
Their horizontal components point toward the centre from opposite sides, so those components cancel.
Because the instrument is wider at the top, the inward normals on both sloping walls have upward components.
Those vertical components point the same way and therefore add.

ai_rubric.observable: States that equal and opposite horizontal components from matching side-wall patches cancel
States that the vertical components from the two sloping walls act upward and add

parts.misconception_target: Asserting that a submerged object has upthrust without tracing how pressure magnitude and surface-normal direction create the whole-surface resultant.
hints: Build a causal chain from greater depth to greater pressure to stronger normal-force contributions.
Combine the plate forces with the side-wall components already analysed in (c).
walkthrough: Hydrostatic pressure grows with depth, so lower regions of the instrument experience greater pressure than upper regions.
Pressure on every surface patch produces a normal force, so lower plates and lower side patches make stronger contributions.
The horizontal components cancel by symmetry, while the vertical components from all surfaces do not cancel completely.
The upward contributions exceed the downward top contribution, leaving an upward resultant called upthrust.

ai_rubric.observable: Links greater depth on lower regions to greater hydrostatic pressure and stronger pressure-force contributions
Concludes that combining all normal pressure forces on the closed surface gives an upward resultant called upthrust
